title: Redirects after you change the URLs
metaTitle: Map old URLs to the closest page
excerpt: Map every old URL you know about to the closest new page. A redesign that responds with a 404 spends the links you already earned and starts over.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground. The two currents fit a piece about sending old URLs across to the closest new page.
caption: The old path should arrive at the new one. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should old URLs go after a redesign?
faqs.answer: To the closest new page that does the same job. A case study goes to the new case study. A retired article goes to the nearest living topic, not to the homepage by default. Use a permanent 301 redirect, and keep the map in the repository so it ships with the new site.

faqs.question: What do you do with pages that no longer exist?
faqs.answer: Choose the closest honest destination and write that choice down. An ended promotion can go to the current offer, and a removed biography can go to the team page. Avoid a thin "we moved" page in the middle. Use the 404 page, with a way forward, only for addresses you do not actually have.

faqs.question: When should the redirect map be removed?
faqs.answer: Leave it. Bookmarks and external links last longer than a launch month. When you change URLs again, point the original path directly at the newest page instead of chaining hops. Check the map before you reuse an old slug for a new page, or the redirect will shadow the publish.

markdown:
Website redirects after redesign are a map from every old URL you know about to the closest new page. A redesign that answers those URLs with a 404 starts over. The links you already earned, in search, in old emails, in partner sites, and in someone's bookmarks, are part of the site. They are not a side effect you get to discard because the information architecture is cleaner.

Build the map before you launch. Launching without it is a decision to throw away the paths people already use.

## Make the list before you design the new paths

Collect the URLs that exist, not only the ones you remember. The current sitemap. The navigation. The obvious patterns, such as `/blog/the-old-slug` and `/work/client-name`. The addresses in your analytics for the last year, if you have them. The addresses you have printed on a PDF, a sponsor page, or an email signature. Search for the domain and see which paths other sites point at.

Write them in a sheet with two columns: old, and the closest new page. Closest means the page that now does that job. A case study moves to the new case study. A service page moves to the service page. A post you are keeping moves to the new post URL. A post you are retiring moves to the nearest topic that still exists, or to a short note that explains the retirement, not to the homepage by default.

The homepage is the wrong target for most of the list. It is closest only when the old page was genuinely the home page, or when there is no nearer page and you have accepted that the specific promise is gone. Sending every retired URL to `/` trains people to ignore your links. They land on a general introduction and have to search again for the thing the old URL named.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) describes a warning sign that applies here: a page that leaves someone feeling they need to search again to get the information. A redirect to the closest page avoids that. A 404, or a redirect to a vague home, creates it. The person followed a specific link. Meet the specificity as far as the new site honestly can.

## Permanent redirects, stored with the code

Use a permanent redirect, an HTTP 301, for a move you mean to keep. The old URL should answer with the new location, and the new page should answer as itself. Temporary redirects are for temporary moves. A redesign is not temporary. Marking it temporary "until we are sure" leaves browsers and other tools unwilling to remember the move, and you will still be unsure in six months.

Keep the map in the repository, next to the site, so a change is reviewed like any other change. A redirect file that lives only in a host's dashboard will be forgotten at the next migration. The file can be simple: old path, new path. Generate the host's format from that list if you need to. One source.

Watch for chains. Old A to old B to new C costs an extra hop and is easy to get wrong. When you redesign again, point A and B both at C. Update the map. Do not append forever.

Trailing slashes, `www`, and `https` should be decided once and redirected once, at the edge, before the page-level map. If every URL exists in four variants, your map will be a mess and your analytics will split. Pick the canonical form, redirect the others, and write the page map in the canonical form only.

Query strings need a rule. If an old campaign parameter should be ignored, ignore it and redirect to the clean path. If the query changed which page you showed, map the pairs that matter and test them. A redirect that drops a parameter people still use, without meaning to, is a silent 404 inside a 200.

## What "closest" means when the page is gone

Some pages should not come back. A promotion that ended, a role you filled, a draft that was never meant to be linked and was linked anyway. Closest is a judgment. Write it down in the sheet so the judgment is visible.

For an ended promotion, the closest page might be the current offer, with a sentence that the named promotion is over. For a removed article, the closest might be the category or the updated piece. For a personal bio of someone who left, the closest might be the team page, not a lookalike URL that implies they are still there.

Do not redirect a removed page to a thin "we moved" page that only contains a link. That intermediate page is a chain with worse content. Send people to the destination. If you need a sentence of context, put it on the destination or accept that the destination's own headline is the context.

Keep a small set of redirects you expect to be hit, and a long tail. The long tail still matters. One inbound link from a university page or a news mention can be the path a careful buyer uses. It will not show up as a top row in analytics until it 404s and disappears. Map it anyway if you know about it.

The 404 page is for the URLs you truly do not know. Give it a search or a short list of the main sections, and the primary way to contact you. A styled 404 that offers nothing is a dead end with better type. Log the misses for a few weeks after launch and add the ones that are clearly old URLs of yours. The map can grow after launch. It should not start empty.

## Launch week

Ship the redirects in the same release as the new URLs. A gap of a day, while the new site is live and the map is "coming," is a day of 404s on every old link. If the new paths are not ready, the old site should stay up. Order the work so the map and the pages arrive together.

Test a sample from the sheet, and test the ones you are proud of plus the ones that look boring. Request the old path and confirm you land on the new page, once, with a 301, and that the final page returns 200. Click the primary action there. A redirect to a page that itself 404s is a broken map, not a successful status code.

Check a phone and a desktop browser, because caches will hold an old redirect during the test. Use a fresh session when a result surprises you. Confirm `http` and the non-www host if those were ever public. Confirm a URL that had a trailing slash and one that did not.

Tell the team the old URLs are intentionally retired and forwarded. Otherwise someone will "fix" a 301 by recreating the old path as a duplicate page. Duplicates split the map and confuse the next editor. The redirect is the fix.

## After the redesign has settled

Leave the map in place. Removing redirects after a few months punishes anyone with a slow bookmark and any site that updates its links on a human schedule. Disk space for a list of paths is cheap. Lost trust on a partner's resources page is not.

When you add a new page later, do not reuse a path you are still redirecting without removing the redirect on purpose. A redirect that shadows a new page is a bug that looks like "the CMS ignored my publish." Check the map when you choose a slug.

Review the 404 log at the end of the first month. Add the misses that are yours. Ignore the noise from bots that request paths you never had. The goal is not a perfect historical record of every typo. The goal is that a real old URL, the kind a person would follow, lands on the closest living page.

If you change URLs again inside the new site, update the original map and add the new hop as a direct jump. Future you, and the next studio, should be able to read the file and see where a path went. A comment on a row that says why a page was retired will save a meeting.

## A sheet you can finish before launch

- Every URL in the old sitemap has a row.
- High-traffic and known inbound URLs have rows even if they were not in the sitemap.
- Each row points at the closest page, not the homepage by habit.
- The file in the repo is the one the host uses.
- A sample of old URLs returns 301 and then 200.
- The 404 page offers a way forward, and someone owns the log for a month.

Image weight is the next way a careful redesign gets slow without meaning to. [Image weight on a photography-heavy page](/blog/image-weight-on-a-photography-heavy-page) is the piece to read next. A beautiful photograph can still be the wrong number of bytes. The redirect map will not save a page that takes too long to show the picture people came to see.

You can judge a redesign by whether the old paths still make sense. Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) with that in mind: the current page should be the one an older link deserves to open.
